forms.text: For a measurable space (Ω,F), a discrete-time filtration is a family (F_n)_{n≥0} of sub-σ-algebras of F such that F_n⊆F_m whenever n≤m.

mathematical_review: ProofWiki separately sources the discrete-time filtered measurable space construction: sub-σ-algebras are indexed by time, and inclusion is nondecreasing. The filtration does not itself require a probability measure; when paired with a probability space it forms a filtered probability space. This is not the complete, right-continuous or usual-conditions filtration. The direct continuous-time filtration locator was not accessible in this session and requires renewed source inspection before any additional continuous-time variant can be source-ingested.

context: Discrete time or continuous-index adaptedness to a filtration

forms.text: A real-valued process (X_n)_{n≥0} adapted to a filtration (F_n)_{n≥0} satisfies that X_n is F_n-measurable for every nonnegative integer n.
A real-valued process (X_t)_{t≥0} adapted to a filtration (F_t)_{t≥0} satisfies that X_t is F_t-measurable for every real t≥0.

mathematical_review: ProofWiki separately displays discrete and continuous-time adapted-process definitions. Their structural shared meaning is measurability of X at each time with respect to information up to that time, but the different index sets remain separately labeled. An adapted process need not be a martingale, Markov process, or have sample-path continuity. Filtration and measurable-random-variable foundations remain independent prerequisites.

context: Integrable real random variable and sub-σ-algebra of the probability space

forms.text: For an integrable real random variable X on (Ω,F,P) and a sub-σ-algebra G⊆F, a version of E[X|G] is an integrable G-measurable random variable Z satisfying ∫_A Z dP = ∫_A X dP for every A∈G. It is unique up to almost-sure equality.

mathematical_review: ProofWiki defines the σ-algebra-conditioned conditional expectation by integrability, G-measurability and matching integrals over each event A∈G; essential uniqueness is a separate theorem. The object is a random variable defined up to almost-sure equality, not a single number. Martingale equations are equality almost surely of such conditional expectation versions. This is not the simpler discrete expectation conditioned on a single positive-probability event.

context: Simple graph vertex coloring with adjacent endpoints distinct

forms.text: A proper vertex k-coloring of a simple graph G=(V,E) is a map c:V→{1,…,k} such that c(u)≠c(v) for every edge {u,v}∈E.

mathematical_review: The accessible ProofWiki Proper Vertex Coloring page explicitly defines the mapping to a palette of k colors and requires adjacent vertices receive unequal colors. The palette may have unused colors, and this is a vertex-coloring concept distinct from edge coloring. The chromatic number is the minimum k that admits such a coloring, so the source-screened proper coloring meaning will provide an exact noncircular prerequisite when separately reviewed.

context: Measurable-state-valued random variables indexed by a set

forms.text: For a probability space (Ω,F,P), a measurable state space (E,Ecal), and an index set I, a stochastic process is an I-indexed family (X_i)_{i∈I} of E-valued random variables on Ω.

mathematical_review: The accessible ProofWiki formal definition allows an arbitrary index set and measurable state space. Sequences indexed by nonnegative integers and real-time indexed processes are special cases. The state-space measurability requirement is essential; merely taking an arbitrary family of functions without measurability would not satisfy the usual definition. Adaptedness is a separate property relative to a filtration.
